originalTitle: Zero-Day Option Traders Are Betting Against Big S&P 500 Swings
summary: While some investors position for AI earnings, geopolitics and interest rates to send stocks either to new highs or into a tailspin, zero-day option traders have increasingly bet that the S&P 500 Index will remain calm.
content:
(Bloomberg) -- While some investors position for AI earnings, geopolitics and interest rates to send stocks either to new highs or into a tailspin, zero-day option traders have increasingly bet that the S&P 500 Index will remain calm.

An analysis of 0DTE options flow from UBS Group AG derivatives strategist Kieran Diamond shows a marked shift toward tactical traders buying calls and selling puts when the market declines, and doing the opposite during rallies. The net effect of what they term a "counter-trend delta bias" is the equivalent of buying low and selling high, which further suppresses swings on the S&P 500.

Zero-day to expiry options have taken on an outsized importance in the daily moves of the equities gauge, with around 66% of the overall volume expiring within a day, according to Garrett DeSimone at OptionMetrics. That's increased the focus on short-term positioning as both retail and institutional traders seek insight on how options flows are influencing the $66 trillion US benchmark index.

"This counter-trend trading pattern seems to be a response to very rangebound markets," said Diamond. "The magnitude of these options flows means that this can start to look self-fulfilling, with options investors helping to limit price moves in either direction."

This intraday tactical shift since 2024 is notable, with larger volumes trading on smaller moves, helping limit S&P 500 realized volatility. The pattern resembles the stabilizing effect of positive gamma, with traders buying into dips and selling into rallies, much like option dealers who are long gamma and similarly buy declines and sell rallies to stay delta-neutral.

The counter-trend trading bias is one factor that has helped contain moves. Another is the long option-dealer gamma regime often seen in the S&P 500, much of which is driven by the prevalence of a big institutional trader selling one-day iron condors — a put spread and a call spread.

RELATED: Popular Zero-Day Trades Curb Stock Rallies: Options Watch

The growth of the 0DTE counter-trend trading flow is now so great that the net effect outweighs the impact from the option dealer re-hedging, according to UBS.

To be sure, the pattern could change if the market has an extended selloff, beyond the AI-focused declines that pushed the S&P 500 down 1.2% on Thursday.

"While the counter-trend flow has so far been very consistent, there's nothing to stop this dynamic reversing in a period of higher volatility," Diamond said. "If 0DTE investors decide to instead chase a move lower by buying puts, then their flows could exacerbate the move, and also leave market makers managing short gamma risks."

While the impact on the S&P 500 has been to suppress moves, some of the short-term trading in the technology sector, for instance, has had the opposite effect. That's given rise to successful intraday momentum strategies with flows tending more to exacerbate rallies and declines.

RELATED: Leveraged ETF Boom Boosts Intraday Momentum Plays: Options Watch

"Dealer hedging associated with 0DTE options can reinforce intraday momentum or contribute to mean reversion, depending on the prevailing gamma environment," said Adrien Geliot, chief executive officer of Premialab. "We saw strong performance from semiconductor-focused intraday momentum strategies during the April–June rally, while the current interest in SPX reversal signals highlights how these dynamics can differ across market conditions."

He added that the number of live strategies for that segment in Premialab's QIS database has increased 50% since the end of March 2025.

"The key challenge is translating these signals into strategies that can capture these effects consistently, while accounting for execution costs," Geliot said.

In general, the demand for option positioning insight is growing, with more retail platforms entering the space and providing market color. Each has its own methodology to map intraday option Greeks — the gamma, vanna and charm metrics that signal how traders and dealers may need to act — with the aim of giving an edge to market speculators.

The boom in 0DTE trading has only increased the relevance of positioning as an important technical driver of intraday price action. The delta-adjusted notional value in the S&P 500 option complex now easily surpasses the average daily volume in the E-Mini futures — a sign that the options "tail" is at times wagging the stocks "dog."

The greater access to data and client demand for insight has driven some institutional providers to refine their estimates of net dealer positioning. While early frameworks generally assumed that all calls were sold by end clients and all puts were bought, newer models are more sophisticated.

JPMorgan Chase & Co. derivatives strategists recently wrote that they have moved away from a proxy for S&P 500 gamma positioning based on open interest to a more flow-based approach using the Cboe Global Markets Inc. data that provide a granular breakdown of whether each option transaction was bought or sold by clients.
